concepts.label: The Spheres of the Earth System
concepts.cardText: Life on Earth is powered by a constant flow of energy and matter. The Sun is the main source of energy, and the Earth's hot interior and chemical reactions in the air, water and rocks also drive the flow of energy and matter. The chapter considers these processes together as belonging to one Earth system made up of interacting spheres. The geosphere is the solid rocks, soil, landforms and the Earth's interior. The hydrosphere is liquid water in the form of oceans, rivers, lakes and groundwater. The cryosphere is the solid form of water, such as ice and snow, like the Himalayan glaciers and polar ice caps. The atmosphere is the air surrounding the Earth that we breathe. The biosphere is all living organisms and their habitats, including mangroves, forests, farms, ocean plankton and coral reefs. Natural processes such as heating by solar radiation, movement of air and water, and nutrient cycling connect these spheres in a delicate balance.

concepts.label: Interactions Among the Spheres
concepts.cardText: From Activity 13.1 we can infer that a disturbance in one sphere can lead to changes in others. For example, less snowfall in winters may lead to less water in the lake in summers, resulting in less water to support the growth of grass. On a large scale, warmer Arabian Sea water leads to more evaporation from the sea, which causes fluctuations in the southwest monsoon and variability in rainfall, bringing floods to some regions of India while leaving others in drought. The rise in atmospheric temperature could eventually accelerate the melting of glaciers and polar ice in the cryosphere, which may lead to the flooding of low-lying regions and, in the long run, raise sea levels and threaten coastal cities. This could disturb the ecosystems within the biosphere by causing habitat loss.

concepts.label: Solar Radiation and the Electromagnetic Spectrum
concepts.cardText: Solar radiation is the main source of energy on the Earth and reaches it as electromagnetic (EM) waves that travel through a vacuum at the speed of light. EM waves cover a wide range of frequencies, from high frequency or short wavelength radiation (gamma rays and X-rays) to low frequency or long wavelength radiation (infrared and radio waves); the high frequency EM waves have very high energy and can be harmful for life. The solar radiation reaching the Earth is concentrated mainly in the ultraviolet (UV), visible and infrared (IR) range, about 99 per cent of the Sun's energy. Short wavelength UV radiation is mostly absorbed by the ozone layer, protecting life and contributing to some atmospheric heating. Visible light reaches the surface, provides energy for photosynthesis, the primary source of food for most organisms, and partly warms the land and water. Infrared radiation warms the Earth's surface, which then re-radiates this heat into the atmosphere; a portion of this outgoing heat is trapped by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour, keeping the Earth warm enough to support life.

concepts.label: Insolation and the Solar Constant
concepts.cardText: The amount of the Sun's radiation that reaches the Earth's surface is called insolation, and it is responsible for warming the Earth's surface and its atmosphere. The average amount of solar energy received per unit time per unit area perpendicular to the Sun's rays at the top of the Earth's atmosphere is called the solar constant, which represents the Sun's energy available on the Earth before any absorption, scattering or reflection in the atmosphere. The solar constant is important because it helps scientists understand the Earth's energy balance, climate and weather patterns. Some of this energy is absorbed and scattered by gases, clouds and dust particles in the atmosphere, so the maximum insolation reaching the surface is lower than the solar constant, about 1 kilowatt per square metre under clear sky conditions. India, in the tropical and sub-tropical regions, receives abundant sunlight throughout the year, which drives the southwest monsoon and offers immense potential for solar energy as a renewable and sustainable source. Anna Mani mapped solar insolation across India.

concepts.label: Albedo: How Surfaces Reflect and Absorb Sunlight
concepts.cardText: Different materials absorb and heat up differently under sunlight. Dark surfaces absorb more sunlight, while light coloured surfaces reflect more and remain comparatively cooler; for example dark coloured roads heat up quickly and dark clothes feel hotter than white ones. The fraction of solar radiation reflected by a surface is called its albedo. High albedo surfaces stay cool because they reflect more light, while low albedo ones heat up more quickly as they reflect less and absorb more light. Snow and ice have high albedo, reflecting a large proportion of the incoming solar radiation, which makes polar regions very cold. Surfaces like black soil and ocean water have lower albedo as they absorb more solar radiation, so they are relatively warmer.

concepts.label: Heat Re-radiation and the Urban Heat Island Effect
concepts.cardText: All objects radiate heat. We feel hot inside a concrete house at night in hot summer because of the heat re-radiated by the concrete, whereas traditional houses built with thick mud and wooden walls stay cool because of less re-radiation. Cities are warmer than their surrounding rural areas, especially during summer and at night. Cities have more built-up areas, with buildings of steel, concrete and brick and roads of concrete and asphalt, which absorb solar radiation and retain heat; the re-radiated heat warms cities more than rural areas. This increases energy demand for air conditioning, further stressing urban ecosystems. Rural areas and forests have more vegetation and stay cool through shade and plant transpiration. The urban heat island effect shows how human land use can alter the local climate.

concepts.label: Latitude and the Shape of the Earth
concepts.cardText: The amount of radiation received by a region also depends on its latitude. Because the Earth is spherical, the Sun's rays strike different latitudes at different angles. The Sun's radiation falling on the equatorial region is concentrated over a smaller area, whereas in the polar region it is spread over a larger area. This is why equatorial regions remain relatively warm throughout the year while polar regions experience much colder conditions, creating temperature differences between the equator and the poles. The Earth's spherical shape and the tilt of its axis also give rise to seasons and the changing length of daytime. Thus solar radiation is not evenly distributed across the globe, and this uneven heating drives global winds and ocean currents.

concepts.label: The Atmosphere and Its Layers
concepts.cardText: The air surrounding the Earth is called the atmosphere, and it is held in place by the force of Earth's gravity. It consists mainly of nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%) along with small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide, water vapour and other gases. Nearly all weather phenomena take place in the troposphere, which has an average height of about 12 km and is heated from the Earth's surface; in it temperature decreases with height, and as warm air rises it drives winds and storms. The height of the troposphere is maximum above the equator and lowest above the poles. In the stratosphere (12 to 50 km), where the ozone layer is located, ozone absorbs UV rays and heats up the atmosphere, so temperature rises with height; this calms the layer due to the lack of vertical mixing of air, keeping weather confined to the troposphere. Above are the mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere, which play only a minor role in regulating climate on the surface, and at about 100 km outer space begins.

concepts.label: The Atmosphere, the Greenhouse Effect and Global Warming
concepts.cardText: The atmosphere plays two crucial roles in protecting life on the Earth. Firstly, it partly absorbs the incoming solar radiation: the ozone layer blocks the harmful UV rays, and clouds and other gases absorb some sunlight before it reaches the surface. Secondly, it traps outgoing heat: the Earth's surface absorbs sunlight and re-radiates it in the infrared region, and greenhouse gases like CO2, CH4 and water vapour absorb this re-radiated heat, preventing it from escaping into space. Without the atmosphere the Earth would be too cold for life to survive. However, excess CO2 from human activities enhances the greenhouse effect, causing global warming, which if left unchecked could make the Earth uninhabitable. Venus is hotter than Mercury, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun, because of the atmosphere on Venus, which has led to an uncontrolled greenhouse effect.

concepts.cardText: The ozone layer is vital to life on the Earth because it acts as a protective shield, absorbing harmful UV radiation from the Sun. Increased UV radiation on the Earth can harm living organisms and the ecosystems. A global agreement known as the Montreal Protocol reduced the use of CFCs and the ozone layer is now slowly recovering, showing the power of international scientific cooperation.

concepts.label: Local Winds: Valley and Mountain Breezes
concepts.cardText: Wind is the movement of air from a region of high pressure to a region of low pressure, and these pressure differences are mainly caused by the uneven heating of the Earth's surface by the Sun. Uneven heating also produces local winds such as valley and mountain breezes. During the day the mountain slopes facing the Sun are heated more rapidly than the valley floor, so the air over the slopes becomes warm and rises, creating a low pressure region, and cooler air from the valley moves up the slopes to replace it; this is called a valley breeze. After sunset the situation reverses: the slopes lose heat faster and become cooler while the valley floor remains relatively warmer, so the cooler, denser air over the slopes flows down into the valley; this is a mountain breeze. Such daily changes in wind direction are commonly experienced in hilly regions like Shimla and Dehradun.

concepts.label: Planetary Winds
concepts.cardText: Uneven heating of the Earth between the equator and the poles creates belts of low and high pressure, and this large scale pressure difference sets the air in motion over long distances, giving rise to planetary winds. Near the equator intense heating causes warm air to rise, forming an equatorial low pressure belt. The air moves poleward at higher altitudes, cools, becomes denser and sinks around 30 degrees North and South latitudes, forming the sub-tropical high pressure belts, from which air flows back towards the equator along the surface. Part of the sinking air moves towards the poles along the surface and rises again around 60 degrees North and South, forming the sub-polar low pressure belts. In the polar regions very low temperature causes cold, dense air to sink, forming polar high pressure belts. The Earth's rotation deflects these winds from their straight paths, so planetary winds follow curved paths, to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.

concepts.label: Ocean Currents
concepts.cardText: Ocean currents are the continuous movement of large masses of ocean water. Similar to winds, planetary pressure differences drive the ocean currents: strong planetary winds drag the surface water because of friction, setting surface currents in motion. Differences in temperature and salinity, the rotation of the Earth and the distribution of land masses also influence the movement of ocean water. Warm equatorial waters travel over the surface toward the poles, while colder and denser waters flow back towards the equator through deeper levels. Water with lower salinity, being less dense, tends to remain near the surface, while higher salinity, denser water sinks. The Earth's rotation deflects these moving water masses, forming large circular patterns called gyres, which rotate clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counter clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. By transporting heat from the equator towards the poles, ocean currents reduce temperature differences across the planet and regulate the Earth's climate; the warm North Atlantic Drift keeps many ports ice-free during winter in Europe. Ocean currents also support a massive ecosystem by transporting nutrients.

concepts.label: Biogeochemical Cycles
concepts.cardText: Living organisms constantly exchange matter and energy with the air, water, soil and rocks around them. This continuous interaction between the non-living (abiotic) and living (biotic) components of the Earth results in the transfer of matter and energy across the spheres. It ensures that essential nutrients such as carbon, nitrogen and oxygen are recycled and remain available to support life. This cyclic movement of matter and energy between the abiotic and biotic components is called the biogeochemical cycle. The interconnectedness of ecosystems helps them recover from disturbances or degradation and maintain environmental balance. The chapter examines the water, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen cycles.

concepts.label: The Water Cycle and Climate Change
concepts.cardText: In the water cycle water evaporates from water bodies such as rivers, lakes and oceans and condenses to form clouds. It returns as precipitation in the form of rain, hail or snow and finally flows back to the ocean, and some water seeps through soil and rocks beneath the surface. Climate change is now affecting the water cycle: a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, causing heavier rains in some areas and droughts elsewhere. Melting glaciers add more water to rivers, raising sea levels in the long run and threatening coastal cities such as Mumbai and Chennai. Sudden bursts of intense rainfall result in more run off that erodes soil, and less infiltration reduces the recharge of groundwater, making sustaining agriculture difficult in dry months. concepts.label: The Carbon Cycle
concepts.cardText: Carbon forms the backbone of life; every protein, carbohydrate, fat and DNA molecule contains carbon. It circulates continuously between the atmosphere (CO2), the biosphere (plants and animals), the geosphere (carbonate rocks and fossil fuels) and the hydrosphere (dissolved CO2 and marine shells). In the fast cycle, over days to years, plants convert atmospheric CO2 into glucose using sunlight through photosynthesis, CO2 is released back through respiration, animals eat plants and other animals, and when they die CO2 returns to the air by decomposition. In the slow cycle, over millions of years, dead plants and animals get buried and are converted to fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas; when these are burnt carbon is released back as CO2 on a very short time scale. The ocean water absorbs atmospheric CO2 to form carbonate and bicarbonate ions, which phytoplankton use for photosynthesis and some marine organisms use to form shells. Human activities like burning fossil fuels and deforestation have raised atmospheric CO2 by about 35% since 1960, from 315 ppm to 420 ppm. Some CO2 is necessary to keep the Earth warm enough for life but the balance is critical: excess CO2 intensifies the greenhouse effect, leading to global warming, melting of glaciers and Arctic sea ice, rising sea level and more extreme weather.

concepts.label: The Nitrogen Cycle
concepts.cardText: Nitrogen is an essential element for the synthesis of proteins and nucleic acids in all living organisms. The largest reservoir of nitrogen is the atmosphere, but nitrogen gas (N2) is rather non-reactive and cannot be directly used by plants and animals; it must first be converted to soluble compounds that living beings can absorb. The overall movement of nitrogen between air, soil, water and organisms is the nitrogen cycle, with the steps nitrogen fixation, assimilation, ammonification, nitrification and denitrification. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, such as Rhizobium in the root nodules of legumes and Azotobacter in the soil, convert atmospheric N2 into ammonia. Nitrifying bacteria like Nitrosomonas convert ammonia into nitrite and Nitrobacter convert nitrite into nitrate, a process known as nitrification. Plants assimilate these compounds from the soil, and animals obtain nitrogen by consuming plants or other animals. When plants and animals die or produce waste, decomposers like bacteria and fungi return nitrogen compounds like ammonia to the soil, called ammonification. Denitrifying bacteria such as Pseudomonas convert some nitrates back into nitrogen gas, called denitrification, completing the cycle. Lightning also fixes a tiny amount of nitrogen into nitrogen oxides, and today most nitrogen is fixed artificially by the Haber-Bosch process, which produces most of the fertilisers used today but is energy intensive, and overuse of fertilisers has degraded soil and water.

concepts.label: The Oxygen Cycle
concepts.cardText: Oxygen is one of the Earth's most abundant elements; about 21% of the atmosphere is free oxygen gas (O2), and it is an essential component of most biological molecules like carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids and fats. Oxygen also exists in combined forms, in the Earth's crust as metal oxides and minerals and in the air as carbon dioxide. The oxygen cycle focuses on the processes that regulate the oxygen level in the atmosphere. Organisms like plants and animals use oxygen for respiration and release CO2, and combustion of fuels uses oxygen and releases CO2. Plants restore oxygen through photosynthesis using sunlight, water and CO2 to form glucose and release O2. This balance between consumption (respiration and combustion) and production (photosynthesis) circulates oxygen between the atmosphere, land, oceans and living organisms, sustaining life across all spheres of the Earth.

concepts.label: Human Impact on Earth's Processes
concepts.cardText: Human actions disrupt the biogeochemical cycles across the Earth's spheres. Excess atmospheric CO2 increases ocean absorption, making sea water more acidic, which could threaten tiny plankton and coral reefs and disrupt marine ecosystems; however, warmer ocean water reduces the ocean's capacity to absorb CO2 as an effective carbon sink. Burning of fossil fuels and deforestation saturate natural carbon sinks like forests and oceans, and the excess CO2 intensifies greenhouse warming. The overuse of fertilisers adds excessive nitrogen via nitrates to rivers and lakes, causing widespread growth of algae (algal blooms) that deplete oxygen and kill fish; this process is called eutrophication and threatens water bodies and coastal fisheries. Clearing forests decreases photosynthesis and transpiration, which can lead to a decline in local rainfall, alters surface albedo, increases soil erosion when tree roots no longer hold the soil, and destroys habitats, leading to a decline in biodiversity. Vehicular emissions react with sunlight to form ground level smog and ground level ozone, which is harmful for health, making city air unhealthy.

concepts.label: Restoring the Earth's Balance
concepts.cardText: While human impact affects all the Earth's spheres, a combination of local actions and global cooperation can help restore the Earth's natural systems. The Montreal Protocol has started the recovery of the ozone layer through global cooperation, though the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement, in which countries were supposed to reduce their CO2 emissions, have been less successful. Conserving energy and energy resources, switching to renewable energy resources like solar and wind, planting trees, saving water and practising sustainable farming can help restore the balance. India has planted billions of trees, expanded energy from solar and renewable sources significantly and promoted sustainable farming practices. Individuals can contribute by saving resources (water, food and energy), reducing waste, and reusing and recycling materials. Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment), an India-led global initiative introduced in 2021, encourages people to adopt mindful, eco-friendly lifestyles.

causeLinks.criterion: Connects global cooperation like the Montreal Protocol and local actions like planting trees and renewable energy to restoring the Earth's natural systems.

keyPoints.text: While human impact affects all Earth’s spheres, a combination of local actions and global cooperation can help restore the Earth’s natural systems. For example, the Montreal Protocol has started the process of recovery of the ozone layer through global cooperation.
keyPoints.followUp: What combination of efforts can help recover the Earth's natural systems? Give an example.

checks.criterion: States that a combination of local actions and global cooperation can help restore the Earth's natural systems, e.g. the Montreal Protocol has started the recovery of the ozone layer.

keyPoints.text: However, the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement in which countries were supposed to reduce their CO2 emissions have been less successful.

checks.criterion: States that the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement, in which countries were to reduce CO2 emissions, have been less successful.

keyPoints.text: Conserving energy and energy resources, switching to renewable energy resources (like solar and wind), planting trees, saving water and practising sustainable farming can help restore the balance.
keyPoints.followUp: List steps in daily life and policy that can help restore balance.

checks.criterion: Lists actions that help restore the balance: conserving energy, switching to renewable energy like solar and wind, planting trees, saving water and sustainable farming.

keyPoints.text: Individuals can also contribute by saving resources (water, food and energy). This can be done by reducing waste, reusing and recycling materials.

checks.criterion: States that individuals can contribute by saving resources (water, food and energy), reducing waste, and reusing and recycling materials.

keyPoints.text: Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment), an India-led global initiative introduced at the United Nations Climate Change Conference in 2021, encourages people to adopt mindful, eco-friendly lifestyles.

checks.criterion: States that Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment), an India-led global initiative introduced in 2021, encourages people to adopt mindful, eco-friendly lifestyles.

misconceptions.wrong: All global agreements to reduce emissions have been successful.
misconceptions.fix: The Montreal Protocol has started the recovery of the ozone layer, but the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement have been less successful in reducing CO2 emissions.

verify.quote: While human impact affects all Earth’s spheres, a combination of local actions and global cooperation can help restore the Earth’s natural systems.
For example, the Montreal Protocol has started the process of recovery of the ozone layer through global cooperation.
However, the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement in which countries were supposed to reduce their CO2 emissions have been less successful.
Conserving energy and energy resources, switching to renewable energy resources (like solar and wind), planting trees, saving water and practising sustainable farming can help restore the balance.
Individuals can also contribute by saving resources (water, food and energy).
This can be done by reducing waste, reusing and recycling materials.

Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment), an India-led global initiative introduced at the United Nations Climate Change Conference in 2021, encourages people to adopt mindful, eco-friendly lifestyles.
